newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Belgium misses 1996 budget goal, firm on '97.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Belgium misses 1996 budget goal, firm on '97.

text.p: The Belgian government said on Friday it had failed to reach its self-set 1996 budget deficit target, but vowed to meet its 1997 goals.
"For 1997 we have every hope - even the certainty - that we will reach the 2.9 percent target," Belgian Budget Minister Herman Van Rompuy told a news conference.

The budget and finance ministries said in a statement the 1996 deficit fell to 3.4 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) from 4.1 percent in 1995. Net government borrowing fell to 242.9 billion francs ($7.63 billion) from 290.1 billion in 1995.
Total Belgian government debt fell to 130.2 percent of GDP from 133.7 percent at the end of 1995.

The 1996 budget was drawn up in 1995 with a deficit target of 3.0 percent of GDP. In October 1996, at the presentation of the 1997 budget, this target was revised to 3.3 percent due to disappointing economic growth.

"We did overshoot our target by 0.1 percent, but we are still doing better than other European countries," Van Rompuy said, adding that the average 1996 deficit of European Union member countries was estimated at 4.6 percent.
He also said the 1997 budget was the one which matters for Belgium's membership of the single European currency in 1999.
"It is on the 1997 budget that we will be judged," he said.
Belgian financial markets were unmoved by the news. "Next year's (1997) deficit is more important," one bond trader said. "Whether we reach three percent or not."

The government blamed the overshoot on disappointing economic growth, overspending in the health insurance sector and disappointing receipts from withholding taxes on fixed-income savings instruments.
The Belgian government in December made a first stab at cutting social security overspending by taking 10 billion francs of austerity measures in the health insurance sector.
Van Rompuy said the government's annual budget review would be brought forward to January from the usual February-March to deal with social security overspending.
"At the 1997 budget review at the end of January we will see whether an additional effort is necessary," Van Rompuy said.

Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt told the news conference that withholding tax receipts from fixed income investments such as bonds and savings accounts, at 60 billion francs in the first 11 months of 1996, were 21 percent lower than in the first eleven months of 1995.

He said withholding tax income fell partly because of the fall in interest rates -- which leads to a proportional fall in taxes on interest income -- and partly because of a switch towards tax-free savings instruments such as bank savings book accounts following the increase of withholding tax on fixed income instruments in 1995.
Belgium raised taxes on fixed income investments to 15 percent from 10 percent in 1995.
